q.t: Fill in: Birds ___ fly. (ability)
q.e: Ability → can.

q.t: Fill in: ___ I come in, sir? (polite/formal permission)
q.e: Asking permission formally → May.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ see a doctor about that cough. (advice)
q.e: Advice → should.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ wear a seat belt. It's the law.
q.e: A strong rule/necessity → must.

q.t: Choose the correct sentence.
q.e: A modal takes no -s and is followed by V1 without ‘to’.

q.t: Fill in: When I was five, I ___ ride a bicycle. (past ability)
q.e: Past ability → could.

q.t: Fill in: ___ we go for a walk? (suggestion)
q.e: Suggestions/offers with I/we → Shall.

q.t: Fill in: It ___ rain today. Take an umbrella. (possibility)
q.e: Possibility (maybe) → may.

q.t: Fill in: We ___ respect our elders. (moral duty)
q.e: Moral duty → ought to.

q.t: Which is a polite request?
o: Could you please close the door?
You must close the door at once.
q.e: ‘Could you …?’ is the softest, politest way to ask.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ bring your lunch; food will be served. (not necessary)
q.e: No necessity → needn't. ‘mustn't’ would mean it is forbidden.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ touch that wire. It's live! (forbidden)
q.e: Not allowed → mustn't.

q.t: Fill in: I ___ play cricket every evening, but now I don't.
q.e: A past habit that has stopped → used to.

q.t: Fill in: Yesterday the lift was broken, so we ___ climb the stairs.
q.e: ‘must’ has no past form — use ‘had to’.

q.t: Fill in: He ___ come, but I'm not sure. (weak possibility)
q.e: Weak possibility → might.

q.t: Fill in: ___ you like some tea? (polite offer)
q.e: ‘Would you like …?’ is the polite form for offers.

q.t: Fill in: She ran 10 km. She ___ be tired. (logical certainty)
q.e: We are almost sure from the evidence → must.

q.t: Fill in: ___ you live long! (a wish/blessing)
q.e: Wishes and blessings use ‘May’.

q.t: Find the error: He can drives a car.
q.e: After a modal, use V1: can drive.

q.t: Fill in: After the course, I ___ speak French fluently.
q.e: Two modals can't stand together. For the future of ‘can’, use ‘will be able to’.

q.t: Fill in: The ground is wet. It ___ have rained last night.
q.e: Strong guess about the past from evidence → must have + V3.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ have told me earlier. Now it's too late.
q.e: Criticising a past action that didn't happen → should have + V3.

q.t: Fill in: He ___ have stolen the money — he was with me all day.
q.e: Sure it did not happen → can't have + V3.

q.t: Fill in: She isn't answering. She ___ have gone to sleep.
q.e: A possibility about the past (we are not sure) → may/might have + V3.

q.t: Which sentence shows permission?
q.e: ‘You may leave’ = you are allowed to. ‘It may rain’ shows possibility.

q.t: Choose the correct negative: You must stay. → (it is not necessary)
q.e: The opposite of ‘must’ (necessary) in meaning is ‘needn't’ (not necessary). ‘mustn't’ means ‘not allowed’.

q.t: Fill in: As children, we ___ sit by the river for hours.
q.e: ‘would’ can describe repeated past habits (like ‘used to’).

q.t: Find the error: You ought respect the law.
q.e: ‘ought’ is the one modal that needs ‘to’: ought to respect.

q.t: Fill in: Must I finish this today? — No, you ___.
q.e: ‘No’ answer to ‘Must I?’ means it is not necessary → needn't. ‘mustn't’ would forbid it.

q.t: Fill in: If I had wings, I ___ fly to you.
q.e: An imagined, unreal situation → would.

q.t: Fill in: I ___ have passed if I had studied harder.
q.e: A past possibility that did not happen → could have + V3.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ have bought milk; there's plenty in the fridge.
q.e: You bought it, but it was not necessary → needn't have + V3.

q.t: Choose the sentence that means ‘I am almost sure he forgot’.
q.e: must have + V3 = a strong conclusion about the past.

q.t: Choose the most polite request.
o: Would you mind opening the window?
Open the window, will you, quickly?
Can you open the window for me?
You will open the window now.
q.e: ‘Would you mind …ing?’ steps back the furthest, so it sounds the politest.

q.t: Find the error: She will can finish the work tomorrow.
o: ‘will can’ should be ‘will be able to’
q.e: Two modals never stand together; use ‘be able to’ after ‘will’.

q.t: Fill in: He is very rich; he ___ have a big house. (logical guess about now)
q.e: A confident guess about the present → must.

q.t: Fill in: The guests ___ arrive at any moment, so let's get ready.
q.e: A possibility in the near future → may (or might).

q.t: Which sentence shows a past habit?
o: My grandfather would walk five miles every morning.
My grandfather would walk more if his knees allowed it.
Would you walk with me to the market this evening?
My grandfather will walk five miles tomorrow.
q.e: Repeated past action → ‘would’ like ‘used to’. The others show a condition, a request and the future.

q.t: Fill in: You ___ not have spoken so rudely to her. It hurt her.
q.e: Criticising a past action that did happen → should not have + V3.

q.t: Fill in: I'm not used ___ up so early.
q.e: ‘be used to’ means ‘be accustomed to’; here ‘to’ is a preposition, so it takes -ing. (Unlike ‘used to + V1’ for past habits.)
